title: Tree canopy extent and height change in Europe, 2001-2021, quantified using Landsat data archive
relevance: Continental canopy product that reports its own height-dependent error structure: most mapping error concentrates in the 4-6 m canopy-height interval, and the product underestimates ESA WorldCover tree area by 25% specifically because short and open-canopy stands are omitted. This is independent confirmation of finding 1 - the deficit is a property of canopy mapping at low heights, not of our model - and it locates the transition band at 4-6 m, close to where our recall curve turns over. Gives us a citable precedent for reporting the height at which our product becomes reliable rather than reporting a single accuracy number.

title: Comparison of three global canopy height maps and their applicability to biodiversity modeling: Accuracy issues revealed
relevance: Compares three global canopy-height products against reference height and finds systematic, height-dependent bias in each - two underestimate at all heights, one overestimates low canopy and underestimates tall canopy. Directly relevant because our CHM is the axis we stratify recall on: if the CHM itself is biased by height, part of our monotonic recall curve is CHM error rather than detection failure, which is a caution finding 1 does not currently account for. Argues for validating our 2016 lidar CHM's height accuracy before treating its bands as ground truth.

authors: Ferraz, A., Saatchi, S., Mallet, C. & Meyer, V.
title: Lidar detection of individual tree size in tropical forests
relevance: Reports detection rate explicitly as a function of tree size and canopy stratum, showing detection near-complete for dominant trees and collapsing for suppressed and mid-story trees - the same monotonic shape as our recall-by-CHM-band curve, from a completely different sensor. Establishes that the shape of finding 1 is a general property of remote canopy detection, not an artifact of RGB or of U-Net, which supports finding 2 (architecture is not the constraint). Also supplies the framing of reporting detection as a size-conditional probability rather than a single recall.

authors: Hamraz, H., Contreras, M.A. & Zhang, J.
title: Forest understory trees can be segmented accurately within sufficiently dense airborne laser scanning point clouds
relevance: Partially contradicts the fatalistic reading of finding 1: understory omission is driven by insufficient sampling density, and with dense enough point clouds plus explicit vertical stratification, understory recall rose 22.1% (at a 15.0% precision cost) and understory F-score improved 11.5% while overstory was essentially unaffected. The intervention that works is stratify-then-segment, not a better single-pass model - the direct analogue for us would be a height-band-conditioned model or loss rather than one city-wide model. The precision cost is the honest counterweight: we should expect our low-height recall gains to buy commission error, which is consistent with finding 5's move toward the more liberal NDVI reference.

authors: Clark, A., Phinn, S. & Scarth, P.
title: Pre-processing training data improves accuracy and generalisability of convolutional neural network based landscape semantic segmentation
relevance: Shows that patch sampling systematically under-samples small-area features - features with smaller area are sampled less and therefore classified worse - and that stratified patch sampling fixes it without changing the architecture. This is a mechanism for finding 1 that is entirely under our control: our 2020 training patches almost certainly contain far fewer small-crown pixels than large-crown pixels, so the model is trained to ignore them. Suggests a cheap test before any label overlay work - re-sample training patches stratified by CHM band and see whether low-height recall moves.

title: Nationwide urban tree canopy mapping and coverage assessment in Brazil from high-resolution remote sensing images using deep learning
source: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing 198, 1-15
relevance: Large-scale urban canopy mapping that names its three dominant error modes: missed small-canopy trees, shrub-versus-tree confusion, and over/under-estimation in dense canopy - and states the trade-off plainly, that adding small-crown training examples also pulls in shrubs and low vegetation. That trade-off is the likely explanation for finding 5: our NIR+CHM overlay lifted low-height recall by 0.34 and landed us next to the more liberal NDVI reference because we recruited non-tree vegetation, not only short trees. Argues the 250-point interpretation must distinguish short trees from shrubs explicitly, or it cannot adjudicate this.
